findings.message: The word search control is never built when the top-words list is empty, so a user whose notes have no repeated word of 5+ characters cannot search for specific words at all, even though the notes contain words to search. buildWordsTab: `if (topWords.getWords().isEmpty()) { wordSearchForm.add(new LabelField("(no data)")); return wordSearchForm; }` comes before the "Word search" header, the ShortTextField and the ButtonField. The top list is empty whenever every word of length >= MIN_WORD_LENGTH occurs once (findWords prunes counts < MIN_PHRASE_FREQUENCY), but the specific-word search counts short and single-occurrence words, so it would still return results.

When the top-words list is empty (e.g. every long word occurs only once, or there are only short words), the method returns early and the Word search form is never added. Searching for specific words (including short ones, which the search explicitly supports) would still be meaningful in that case. The search UI should be built whether or not top words exist. Keep word search available when the top-word list is empty If notes contain only short words or no repeated words, `findWords` returns an empty top-word list despite having searchable text. This early return hides the search controls, preventing users from searching those words even though explicit searches support short words and single occurrences. Only skip rendering the rankings, not the search controls.

A search with more than 25 distinct words silently drops the least frequent ones, and the 'combined occurrences' total is understated, because the input limit in the help text is never enforced. WordSearchThread calls `StatisticsUtil.findWords(notesToSearch, searchWords, StatisticsUtil.TOP_N_WORDS)`, and findWords applies `.limit(N)` with N = 25. StatisticsDialog only says "Enter a comma-separated list of 1-25 words" (line 379). WordSearchAction checks only isFormValid (non-blank) and never checks wordSet.size(). showWordSearchResults then sums only the truncated list: `foundWords.getWords().stream().mapToInt(Word::occurrenceCount).sum()`.

The word search passes TOP_N_WORDS (25) as N, so its results are cut off at 25 words. The UI only says '1-25 words' in help text and never enforces it. If a user enters more than 25 words, some found words are silently dropped, and the 'combined occurrences' total in showWordSearchResults is also wrong because it is summed from the truncated list. Either use specificWords.size() (or Integer.MAX_VALUE) as N for searches, or validate the input count. The word search passes TOP_N_WORDS (25) as N, so its results are cut off at 25 words. Validate the parsed search-word count before starting the worker The form only checks for blank text, so comma-only input can produce an empty word set, which `findWords` interprets as a request for the most common words rather than a specific-word search. Likewise, more than 25 parsed words are accepted but silently truncated by the worker, making the reported combined count incomplete. Validate that the parsed set contains 1–25 words before launching the search.

Search terms are matched against normalized note text without being normalized themselves, so a term in a different form (uppercase, trailing punctuation, an internal space, or an apostrophe TagList may change) may never match and is reported as zero occurrences. findWords applies normalizeText to the note text but compares tokens with `specificWords.contains(word)` against the raw set. In the UI that set comes from `TagList.fromRawString(...)` / `tag.getTag()`. TagList is an external Snotes class, and nothing in this repo shows that its normalization matches normalizeText (lowercase, keep apostrophes, non-alphanumerics become spaces). A direct caller passing Set.of("Hello") gets no match.

Search terms are normalized with TagList/Tag rules, not with StatisticsUtil.normalizeText(), which is what the note text goes through. Tag normalization (case, spaces turned into separators, stripped or kept punctuation such as apostrophes or hyphens) does not necessarily match the word tokenizer. So a valid search like "Isn't", "e-mail" or a term with surrounding punctuation can silently return 0 occurrences. A term with spaces (e.g. "hello world") can never match because note text is split on whitespace. Run each term through normalizeText() and split/trim it the same way findWords does. Words with equal counts are ranked in HashMap iteration order, so which words make the top 25 at a tie boundary is arbitrary. This is unlike PhraseList, which has a documented tiebreaker. `.sorted((w1, w2) -> Integer.compare(w2.occurrenceCount(), w1.occurrenceCount()))` followed by `.limit(N)` has no secondary key, and it runs on `wordCounts.entrySet()` of a HashMap.

Sorting uses occurrence count only, with no tiebreaker. Words with equal counts come out in HashMap iteration order, so which words make the top-25 cutoff, and the order in which they are displayed, is arbitrary. PhraseList has a deterministic tiebreaker; add a secondary sort (e.g. alphabetical) here for stable, reproducible results and tests. Sorting uses occurrence count only, with no tiebreaker. Every distinct token is kept in a second HashSet for the unique-word count, which undercuts the memory concern the prune comment cites. The work is also wasted on the specific-word search path, where the dialog never shows the count. `uniqueWords.add(word)` runs for every token before any filtering, so the set holds every distinct word. The later comment justifies pruning by the risk of OutOfMemory on large datasets. showWordSearchResults never reads getUniqueWordCount().

The uniqueWords HashSet keeps every distinct token in the whole corpus for the full scan. The specific-word search path does this too, even though it only needs counts for a handful of words and the dialog never shows the unique count for searches. The comment below mentions OOM concerns for large datasets. This duplicates the unpruned map's memory and repeats the work on every search. Several new tests check only the shape of the output, so they would pass on a broken implementation, for example one that returns an empty list. findWords_shouldLimitResultsToN asserts only `result.getWords().size() <= 3`, which an empty result satisfies. findWords_withNullNoteText_shouldBeIgnored asserts only `assertFalse(result.getWords().isEmpty())`, without checking the words or counts. No test covers the >N specific-words case, WordSearchThread, Word/WordList validation, or the new Phrase wordCount check.

The change tightens the public Phrase record's contract, which the word-statistics feature did not need: it now rejects wordCount 0 and occurrenceCount 0, which the old Javadoc explicitly allowed. The old docs said wordCount was "zero if the phrase is empty" and occurrenceCount "A non-negative integer". The new code throws IllegalArgumentException on `wordCount <= 0` and `occurrenceCount <= 0`. The in-repo callers (findPhrases uses len >= 2 and count >= 2; PhraseListTest uses counts >= 1) still comply, but any external caller that builds a zero-count Phrase now throws.

This is an unrelated behavior change to an existing public record. wordCount == 0 and occurrenceCount == 0 now throw, where they were previously documented as valid (the old javadoc allowed empty phrases with wordCount 0). Any external caller or extension that constructs zero-count phrases will now fail at runtime. It belongs in a separate change, or needs a note in the PR description. The architecture doc still says the loader runs 6 parallel worker tasks, but the change adds a seventh. The unchanged context line reads "Loader runs **6 parallel worker tasks** via `ExecutorService`: general counts, per-year, all-months, per-year+month, day-of-week, and phrase extraction", while StatisticsLoaderThread.run now does `workers.add(this::loadWords);`, which makes 7.

normalizeText keeps every apostrophe, including leading/trailing ones used as single quotes. So 'hello' becomes the token "'hello'", which is counted separately from "hello". A standalone ' becomes its own 'word'. This inflates the new unique-word count, splits occurrence counts in the top-words list, and makes specific-word searches miss quoted occurrences. Word search runs against the notes list captured when the statistics were loaded, so it may give stale counts after the user edits notes. If that list is the live DataManager list, iterating it off the EDT may also race with edits. WordSearchAction builds `new WordSearchThread(stats.getAllNotes(), wordSet)`. Statistics.allNotes is `dataManager.getNotes()` captured in StatisticsLoaderThread.getStatistics(), and StatisticsExtension caches Statistics until an explicit refresh. The repo does not show whether getNotes() returns a copy.
